moduleTitle: The five stages of liberation (five khands) and the barriers to mukti

note.specFocus: Spec 3.1.7.1 Key beliefs: the five stages of liberation (five khands) and barriers to mukti (illusion, self-centredness, lust, anger, greed, worldly attachment, pride).
note.summary:
THE FIVE KHANDS (realms or stages of spiritual development)
Guru Nanak describes five stages on the path to mukti at the end of Japji Sahib (pauris 34–37, Ang 7–8). Many Sikhs see them as stages of inner growth rather than physical places.
1. Dharam Khand – realm of duty/righteousness. God made the earth 'as a home for dharam' (dharamsaal). People realise that their actions are judged and accept moral responsibility.
2. Gian Khand – realm of knowledge. The person gains spiritual knowledge, wondering at the vastness of creation – countless worlds, suns and moons.
3. Saram Khand – realm of effort (sometimes 'spiritual endeavour' or beauty). The mind and intellect are refined and shaped by effort in meditation and good living.
4. Karam Khand – realm of grace. God's grace fills the person with spiritual power; here dwell the great devotees who have overcome haumai. 'In the realm of grace, the Word is power' (Ang 8).
5. Sach Khand – realm of truth: 'In the realm of truth the Formless Lord abides' (Ang 8). The soul is united with God – mukti. Guru Nanak says describing it is 'as hard as steel'.
Notice: effort comes first, but the final stages depend on grace.

BARRIERS TO MUKTI
• Maya – illusion: treating the temporary world (wealth, status, pleasures) as if it were ultimate reality, and forgetting God.
• Haumai – self-centredness/ego: the root barrier (see module 1.6).
• The five thieves (panj chor), which grow from haumai:
 – Kaam – lust; overcome by self-control.
 – Krodh – anger; overcome by patience and forgiveness.
 – Lobh – greed; overcome by contentment (santokh) and sharing.
 – Moh – worldly attachment (to possessions, people, status); overcome by detachment while still living as a householder.
 – Ahankar – pride; overcome by humility (nimrata).
Gurbani describes these thieves breaking into the 'house' of the body. The remedy is nam japna, the Guru's teaching, sewa, the sangat and God's grace.

LIVING THIS OUT
Sikhs do not withdraw from the world to escape maya; they live as householders but try to be 'like a lotus in water' – in the world but not stained by it. Practices such as giving dasvandh, sewa and avoiding intoxicants and adultery (Amrit vows) help guard against the thieves.

DIVERSITY
Some Sikhs read the khands as literal realms; others as psychological stages. There is debate on whether Sach Khand can be reached in this life (jivan mukti) or only after death. Non-religious people may agree that greed, anger and pride are harmful, without linking them to mukti.

KEY TERMS: khand, Dharam/Gian/Saram/Karam/Sach Khand, maya, haumai, panj chor, kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, ahankar.

questions.question:
Which one of the following is the final stage of liberation (the fifth khand)?
A Dharam Khand
B Gian Khand
C Karam Khand
D Sach Khand
questions.modelAnswer: D – Sach Khand, the realm of truth, where the soul is united with God, 'where the Formless Lord abides' (Japji pauri 37, Ang 8). The order is Dharam, Gian, Saram, Karam, Sach.
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Only one is correct; write the letter clearly. If unsure, cross out options you know are wrong first.

questions.question:
Which one of the following is NOT one of the five thieves (barriers to mukti)?
A Kaam (lust)
B Krodh (anger)
C Daya (compassion)
D Lobh (greed)
questions.modelAnswer: C – Daya (compassion). Daya is a virtue. The five thieves are kaam (lust), krodh (anger), lobh (greed), moh (worldly attachment) and ahankar (pride).
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Only one is correct; write the letter clearly. If unsure, cross out options you know are wrong first.

questions.question: Give one barrier to mukti in Sikh teaching.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of: maya (illusion); haumai (self-centredness); kaam (lust); krodh (anger); lobh (greed); moh (worldly attachment); ahankar (pride).
questions.examTip: A 1-mark short response needs one accurate, relevant point only. A short phrase or sentence is enough; do not waste time explaining.

questions.question: Give the meaning of Gian Khand.
questions.modelAnswer: The realm/stage of knowledge – where a person gains spiritual knowledge and understanding of the vastness of God's creation.
questions.examTip: A 1-mark short response needs one accurate, relevant point only. A short phrase or sentence is enough; do not waste time explaining.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which belief in the barriers to mukti influences Sikhs today.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: Sikhs try to control anger (krodh) and lust (kaam). For example, an amritdhari Sikh promises to avoid adultery, and Sikhs try to respond to insults with patience, because these 'thieves' steal a person's spiritual progress.

Second way: Sikhs try to avoid greed (lobh) and attachment (moh) by sharing their wealth. Giving dasvandh (a tenth of income) and offering food in the langar trains them not to cling to money or possessions, which helps them break free from maya.
questions.examTip: Give two separate ways. For each, make a simple point (1 mark) and then develop it with an example, consequence or detail (2 marks). Two undeveloped points score only 2.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which belief in the five khands influences Sikhs today.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: The first stage, Dharam Khand, reminds Sikhs that they live on earth as a place of duty and that their actions will be judged. This encourages them to live responsibly, working honestly and caring for family and community.

Second way: The khands show that the spiritual life is a journey that takes effort and grace. This encourages Sikhs to keep growing – learning more about gurbani (Gian Khand), making effort in meditation and sewa (Saram Khand) – rather than feeling they have 'arrived' just by being born Sikh or attending the gurdwara.
evidence: Dharam Khand – earth as a place for dharam

questions.question:
Explain two of the five stages of liberation (khands).
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Sikh belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First stage: Dharam Khand – the realm of duty or righteousness. God created the earth as a place to practise dharam; here people realise their actions are judged and accept responsibility to live a moral life.

Second stage: Karam Khand – the realm of grace. After effort (Saram Khand), the person receives God's grace and is filled with spiritual power; here live the great devotees who have conquered haumai and are fully devoted to God. This leads to Sach Khand, union with God.

Source: Guru Nanak describes the khands in Japji Sahib, pauris 34–37 (Ang 7–8). Pauri 34 describes God establishing the earth 'as a home for dharam', and pauri 37 says that in the realm of grace 'the Word is power', showing that the final stages depend on God's grace rather than human effort alone.
evidence: Japji pauri 37, Ang 8 – 'Karam khand kee baanee jor'

questions.question:
Explain two Sikh teachings about the barriers to mukti.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Sikh belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First teaching: Maya (illusion) traps people. Maya makes the temporary world of money, status and pleasure seem more real and important than God, so people forget God's Name. Maya is not evil in itself, but attachment to it keeps people in the cycle of rebirth.

Second teaching: The five thieves – lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride – rob a person of spiritual wealth. They grow out of haumai (self-centredness) and make a person manmukh. They are overcome by the opposite virtues and by meditation on God's Name.

Source: Gurbani speaks of the five thieves plundering the 'house' of the body while the person sleeps in ignorance, and of the Name of God as the protection against them. Applying this, Sikhs use nam japna and the support of the sangat to guard against these thieves.
evidence: Five thieves: kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, ahankar

questions.question:
“Anger is the most dangerous of the five thieves.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Sikh teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

Anger (krodh) causes immediate harm to others. In a moment of anger people say cruel things, damage relationships and even commit violence. Because Sikhs believe God's light is in every person, harming someone in anger is an offence against God as well as against them.

Anger destroys the calm mind needed for nam japna. A person filled with anger cannot meditate or be content, so it blocks spiritual progress quickly. Anger also undermines the virtue of patience and the ideal of God as Nirvair (without hatred), which Sikhs aim to reflect.

Anger can also be used to justify injustice. Sikhs are called to defend the oppressed, but if this is done out of anger rather than justice, it becomes revenge, not dharam.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

Many Sikhs would say that ahankar (pride) or haumai is more dangerous, because it is the root of all the other thieves. The Guru Granth Sahib calls haumai a 'chronic disease' (Ang 466). Anger usually comes from pride – feeling one's ego has been insulted – so dealing with pride deals with anger too.

Others might say moh (attachment) or lobh (greed) is more dangerous because it is less obvious. Anger is easy to recognise and regret, but attachment to wealth, status or family can quietly fill a whole life without the person noticing that they have forgotten God. Greed also drives injustice on a large scale, such as exploitation of workers or the environment.

It can be argued that the five thieves are equally dangerous because they work together, and that the real danger is maya, the illusion that the world matters more than God. A non-religious thinker might add that anger is sometimes healthy, motivating people to fight injustice.

CONCLUSION

Anger is very dangerous because of the visible harm it does. However, Sikh teaching sees haumai and pride as the deeper root from which anger and the other thieves grow. So the stronger conclusion is that pride/ego is the most dangerous, and anger is one of its most destructive expressions.
evidence: 'Haumai deeragh rog hai, daaroo bhee is maahi' – Ang 466

questions.question:
“It is impossible to reach Sach Khand in this life.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Sikh teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

Sach Khand is the final realm of truth where the soul is united with the Formless God (Japji pauri 37, Ang 8). Guru Nanak says describing it is 'as hard as steel', suggesting it is far beyond ordinary experience. Most people struggle every day with the five thieves and haumai, so complete union with God may seem impossible while still living in a body.

Many Sikhs think of mukti as ending the cycle of rebirth, which happens at death. On this view a person may make progress through Dharam, Gian and Saram Khand during life, but Sach Khand is only fully reached when the soul leaves the body and merges with God.

Since mukti depends on God's grace (Ang 2), no person can guarantee reaching Sach Khand by their own effort in this life.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

Sikhism teaches jivan mukti – liberation while alive. The Guru Granth Sahib describes the jivan mukt as one who lives in the world but is free from ego and constantly absorbed in God's Name. If this is possible, then reaching Sach Khand, at least as a spiritual state, is possible in this life.

Sikhs believe the ten Gurus were fully united with God while alive, and the Guru Granth Sahib includes the writings of bhagats such as Kabir and Ravidas, who are seen as having realised God. These examples show it can be done.

Many Sikhs interpret the khands not as places but as stages of spiritual development. Sach Khand is then a state of mind – complete God-centredness (gurmukh) – that can be reached through nam japna, sewa and grace. Humanists, by contrast, would say there is no Sach Khand at all, so the question does not arise.

CONCLUSION

Reaching Sach Khand is clearly extremely difficult and depends on God's grace, so it is not something most people achieve. But Sikh teaching on jivan mukti and the example of the Gurus show it is not impossible. The better view is that Sach Khand can be reached in this life by a few, through grace and devotion, and that all Sikhs are called to move towards it now.
